point_1: The town’s funds outside the budget took in more than they spent in 12 of 13 years, and what they hold multiplied 3.6×.
point_2: 34% of what those funds hold is pandemic-era money, and this series ends before we can see whether it has gone.
point_3: Most of the money held outside the budget is not school money — a large part is water, sewer and trash.
point_4: FY23 was the first year since FY17 that the school funds spent more than they took in.

title: Monty Tech — the assessment, and what sets it
points: The state requires Lunenburg to pay $14,605,342 for schools, split between two districts. | Monty Tech billed Lunenburg $1,334,521, which is not what a place there costs. | The Monty Tech bill came in at $1,334,521; a forecast that grew it like a cost said $1,005,464.
point_1: The state requires Lunenburg to pay $14,605,342 for schools, split between two districts.
point_2: Monty Tech billed Lunenburg $1,334,521, which is not what a place there costs.
point_3: The Monty Tech bill came in at $1,334,521; a forecast that grew it like a cost said $1,005,464.

point_2: Paraprofessional FTE the state does not code to special education rose 34.0, FY2020 to FY2025.
point_3: What the schools budget for special education paraprofessionals rose 108.4%.

title: Parks & Recreation — the department, its fund, its sales, its grounds
points: The parks’ own fee fund held $84,818 at 31 March 2026 — 60% of the $140,759 voted for the year. | The fund stood at $10,019 in FY2011, fell to $0 in FY2015, and was $91,726 by 30 June 2025. | The registration system recorded $47,784 in FY2025: 650 programme places and 164 beach passes.
figures: $141k | $85k | $48k | 50% | $84,818 in the Park Revolving Fund, 31 March 2026 | $91,726 | $47,784 recorded by MyRec, 1 July 2024 to 30 June 2025
point_1: The parks’ own fee fund held $84,818 at 31 March 2026 — 60% of the $140,759 voted for the year.
point_2: The fund stood at $10,019 in FY2011, fell to $0 in FY2015, and was $91,726 by 30 June 2025.
point_3: The registration system recorded $47,784 in FY2025: 650 programme places and 164 beach passes.

title: Teacher contracts
points: The contract is the biggest lever the town has not yet pulled: each half a point off the next settlement is $66,741 off the FY28 gap, every year after too. | 2.2 FTE — Held to the cap by attrition instead of at the table, the line sheds 2.2 positions a year — 14% of the staff in ten. | A settlement at the cap shrinks the gap and does not close it: raises of 2.5% instead of 3.4% would have made next year’s gap $619k rather than $930k, and FY32’s $3.39M rather than $3.76M.
point_1: The contract is the biggest lever the town has not yet pulled: each half a point off the next settlement is $66,741 off the FY28 gap, every year after too.
point_2: 2.2 FTE — Held to the cap by attrition instead of at the table, the line sheds 2.2 positions a year — 14% of the staff in ten.
point_3: A settlement at the cap shrinks the gap and does not close it: raises of 2.5% instead of 3.4% would have made next year’s gap $619k rather than $930k, and FY32’s $3.39M rather than $3.76M.

title: School staffing — did it go up, and over which years
points: In 95 of 171 pairs of published years the state counts fewer teachers at the end. | 6.70 teaching staff for every hundred pupils, near the bottom of the state’s comparison group.
figures: 95 pairs of published years, of 171 | 6.70 for every 100 pupils
point_1: In 95 of 171 pairs of published years the state counts fewer teachers at the end.
point_2: 6.70 teaching staff for every hundred pupils, near the bottom of the state’s comparison group.

title: How many students one special education group may have
points: A substantially separate group may not exceed 8 students to one certified special educator. | The rule sets 0 limits on adults in a room; it is a minimum, and IEPs add on top. | DESE reports 41 of Lunenburg’s 258 students with disabilities as substantially separate.
figures: 8 students | 0 limits on adults in the room | 41 children
point_1: A substantially separate group may not exceed 8 students to one certified special educator.
point_2: The rule sets 0 limits on adults in a room; it is a minimum, and IEPs add on top.
point_3: DESE reports 41 of Lunenburg’s 258 students with disabilities as substantially separate.

title: State aid — the part nobody here votes on
points: Roughly a third of the school budget is not Lunenburg’s decision, and the budget book never says so. | Over five years the aid Lunenburg actually received differed from the aid its tax rate was set on by $245,751 in an average year. | In 4 of 5 years the state-aid surprise was in the town’s favour — the direction is far steadier than the size. | The state decides both halves of the minimum: what it pays, and what Lunenburg must. | Where it can be measured, Chapter 70 grew +4.47% a year — more than double what the projection assumes.
point_1: Roughly a third of the school budget is not Lunenburg’s decision, and the budget book never says so.
point_2: Over five years the aid Lunenburg actually received differed from the aid its tax rate was set on by $245,751 in an average year.
point_3: In 4 of 5 years the state-aid surprise was in the town’s favour — the direction is far steadier than the size.
point_4: The state decides both halves of the minimum: what it pays, and what Lunenburg must.
point_5: Where it can be measured, Chapter 70 grew +4.47% a year — more than double what the projection assumes.

title: What courses actually ran, subject by subject
points: Lunenburg High ran 247 sections in SY2025 against 225 in SY2017, on flat enrolment. | 57.8% of Lunenburg High students took a foreign language in SY2025, against 70.1% in SY2017. | 29.3% of Lunenburg Middle School took a world language in SY2025, against 61.0% in SY2023.
point_1: Lunenburg High ran 247 sections in SY2025 against 225 in SY2017, on flat enrolment.
point_2: 57.8% of Lunenburg High students took a foreign language in SY2025, against 70.1% in SY2017.
point_3: 29.3% of Lunenburg Middle School took a world language in SY2025, against 61.0% in SY2023.

title: What a family actually pays
points: Two high schoolers, one sport each, the bus and a club: $1,110 a year. | Three children playing one sport each pay $812.50 a year at the full rate. | A second child adds $460 to a family’s school bill.
point_1: Two high schoolers, one sport each, the bus and a club: $1,110 a year.
point_2: Three children playing one sport each pay $812.50 a year at the full rate.
point_3: A second child adds $460 to a family’s school bill.

title: What other districts spend, for each pupil
points: Lunenburg spends $18,027 for each pupil, all funds — $5,493 below the state median of $23,520. | Lunenburg’s average teacher salary is $97,233, near the top of the neighbouring districts. | Monty Tech spends $25,827 a pupil to Lunenburg’s $18,027 — $7,800 more.
figures: $18,027 | $97,233 | $7,800 more for each pupil at Monty Tech
point_1: Lunenburg spends $18,027 for each pupil, all funds — $5,493 below the state median of $23,520.
point_2: Lunenburg’s average teacher salary is $97,233, near the top of the neighbouring districts.
point_3: Monty Tech spends $25,827 a pupil to Lunenburg’s $18,027 — $7,800 more.

title: What out-of-district special education costs, and what comes back
points: 39.3% of what Lunenburg spent teaching children at other schools came from outside the budget. | $471,771 came off the bill in FY2026 before the state reimbursed anything. | $1,205,949 was spent teaching children at other schools in FY2025.
point_1: 39.3% of what Lunenburg spent teaching children at other schools came from outside the budget.
point_2: $471,771 came off the bill in FY2026 before the state reimbursed anything.
point_3: $1,205,949 was spent teaching children at other schools in FY2025.

title: What sports cost, and who pays
points: $602,285 left the town’s accounts for athletics in FY2024, more than any document totals. | The town’s books code $518,334 to athletics in FY2026, director and trainer included. | $87,822 budgeted for athletic buses in FY2025, more than double the year before.
point_1: $602,285 left the town’s accounts for athletics in FY2024, more than any document totals.
point_2: The town’s books code $518,334 to athletics in FY2026, director and trainer included.
point_3: $87,822 budgeted for athletic buses in FY2025, more than double the year before.

title: What stopped being funded
points: 93 of 132 things cut to zero in the school budget were funded again later. | Everything the schools cut and never funded again carried $181,180. | The two biggest lasting falls in the school budget sit $789,633 a year below their peaks.
point_1: 93 of 132 things cut to zero in the school budget were funded again later.
point_2: Everything the schools cut and never funded again carried $181,180.
point_3: The two biggest lasting falls in the school budget sit $789,633 a year below their peaks.

title: What the state requires us to spend — and where that puts us
points: The state minimum rose 25.2% since FY2018; spending rose 11.9%. | Matching the middle district in the state would take $2,534,627 more than Lunenburg spent. | Lunenburg spent at or above the middle district in 14 of 31 years measured.
point_1: The state minimum rose 25.2% since FY2018; spending rose 11.9%.
point_2: Matching the middle district in the state would take $2,534,627 more than Lunenburg spent.
point_3: Lunenburg spent at or above the middle district in 14 of 31 years measured.

title: When a grant ends — who picks up the bill
points: 42.2% of the grant money that ran out in FY2025 was replaced by the town’s own money. | Employee insurance: $485,010 reported in FY2024; $3,286,872 the year before, $3,511,566 after. | The town now carries $2,520,227 a year that outside money used to, at today’s spending.
point_1: 42.2% of the grant money that ran out in FY2025 was replaced by the town’s own money.
point_2: Employee insurance: $485,010 reported in FY2024; $3,286,872 the year before, $3,511,566 after.
point_3: The town now carries $2,520,227 a year that outside money used to, at today’s spending.

point_2: 97 Lunenburg children are at Monty Tech, the largest single destination.
